Issued at 250 PM CDT Thu Sep 24 2026

LATE AFTERNOON AND TONIGHT:

A broad area of isentropic lift stretched from southwest to 
northeast Minnesota early this afternoon along and ahead of a 
shortwave trough which stretched from far northwest Ontario into
southern Minnesota. A lobe of 500 mb vorticity was positioned 
ahead of the mid-level trough axis. Isentropic moisture 
convergence was maximized over portions of central and northeast
Minnesota, co-located with the returns on the regional radar 
mosaic. Precipitation intensities were a little lighter than 
indicated on radar due to bright band effects from a melt layer 
between 9.5 and 12 kft AGL. This effect is most noticeable at 
and beyond 80 statute miles (70 nautical miles) from KDLH.

Forcing for ascent will persist through this evening although 
the mid-level forcing will push ahead of the low-level ascent 
which will allow the light rain to taper off to drizzle. High-
res guidance points to isolated to scattered showers developing 
late this afternoon and persisting into the evening to the west 
of the area of light rain. That would include much of central 
and north-central Minnesota. Precipitation gradually tapers off 
tonight as the shortwave trough departs. Fog may develop 
tonight, particularly for areas where rain fell today. The fog 
may be locally dense in spots. Overnight lows will be in the 
upper 40s to low 50s.

FRIDAY:

Blocking low pressure will take shape over the New England 
coast. That feature will shunt the shortwave trough toward the 
north as it departs. Partly to mostly cloudy skies are forecast 
for Friday as ridging aloft builds over the northern Plains and 
Canadian Prairies. Isentropic lift will persist over central and
north-central Minnesota which will keep skies mostly cloudy. 
Farther east clouds will gradually clear during the day. 
Temperatures will be near normal where clouds linger to 10-15 
degrees above normal where sunshine is more abundant. Highs will
be in the middle 60s to low 70s. Light winds Friday night 
should allow areas of fog to develop. Fog may be locally dense 
in some spots.

SATURDAY:

Another shortwave trough will move into the region for 
Saturday. Rain chances increase gradually over our Minnesota 
zones. High pressure to our east will once again make the 
eastward progression of precipitation difficult as dry air will 
undercut the precipitation aloft. The greatest rain chances are 
late Saturday afternoon through early Saturday evening west of a
line from Aitkin to International Falls. Rain chances will 
persist through the night as the trough pushes eastward. Rain 
amounts will be light, up to around a tenth of an inch over our 
western areas to a trace farther east. Clouds and showers will 
limit temperatures for central and north-central Minnesota on 
Saturday with highs in those areas in the low to middle 60s. 
Farther east expect upper 60s to low 70s.

The aforementioned blocking low will remain in place over the 
New England coast with a Rex Block expected to develop over the 
eastern CONUS and eastern Canada.

Northeast winds are forecast over the southwest arm of Lake 
Superior which will increase the risk of rip currents for the 
beaches of the Twin Ports Saturday afternoon and evening.

SUNDAY THROUGH NEXT WEEK:

The Rex Block remains in place to our east for the first half 
of next week. This will keep an upper-level ridge positioned 
just to our east while upstream flow slows down. A longwave 
trough is forecast to move into the northern Plains and Canadian
Prairies Monday night into Tuesday which may bring another 
chance of showers to the Northland. A possible complicating 
factor is the poleward moisture stream from Hurricane Polo. 
Moisture from that system could slip around the southern 
periphery of the Rockies and spill into the Plains and Midwest 
ahead of the Tuesday system which could set the stage for 
greater rain chances as the trough moves into our area. Models 
struggle to handle the breakdown of blocking patterns once they 
are established. We will need to keep an eye on that time frame
in case the potential for widespread precipitation emerges.
